list.listitem: Patients with Morton's neuroma typically present with interdigital plantar foot pain that becomes worse with walking. They also have pain with pressure to the intermetatarsal space and may have a Mulder's click on exam. C
Diagnosis is clinical; ultrasound may be useful. C
Conservative treatment for 6 months is successful for approximately 50% of patients. B
A corticosteroid injection may be effective for persistent symptoms. B
Nerve excision successfully reduces foot pain in 80% of patients who fail to respond to other treatments. B

background.definition: Morton's neuroma, also known as an interdigital neuroma, is not a true neuroma but a compression neuropathy of the common digital nerve as it passes between the metatarsal heads. The nerve between the third and fourth metatarsals is most commonly affected.

list.listitem: The incidence of Morton's neuroma is widely unknown.
The only large-scale, population-based study was conducted across 253 UK general practices between 1992 and 2000. The study reports an incidence rate of 46 for men and 86 for women per 100.000.
Morton's neuroma typically occurs in patients aged between 40 and 60 years.
The female to male ratio for Morton's neuroma is 5:1.
The most common location is the third interspace.
Bilateral foot involvement occurs in approximately 2% of patients.
In one case series of 279 treated feet, multiple interdigital neuromas were found in 65.2% of cases.
Compression of the interdigital nerve by either the overlying transverse metatarsal ligament or an inflamed intermetatarsal bursa.
Tight shoes have been implicated in causing Morton's neuromas, but the exact etiology is not understood.
There is no clear consensus regarding pathologic changes in plantar nerves.

There are no noted differences in the nerves of asymptomatic control patients vs. patients with Morton's neuroma with respect to nerve enlargement, blood vessel changes, or nerve fibrosis upon histological examination.
Key history findings include interdigital plantar foot pain that increases with walking, paresthesias in the toes, and numbness. C
Typical physical examination findings include the presence of a Mulder's click, pain with digital pressure to the intermetatarsal space, and sensory loss in the affected toes. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Pain on bony palpation, history of repetitive stress to the forefoot (eg, new running program)
Pain located under one or more metatarsal bones. No paresthesias. Negative radiology test results
Tenderness and swelling directly over the metatarsophalangeal joint on physical examination

list.listitem: Morton's neuroma is most common in middle-aged women and is exacerbated by wearing narrow, high-heeled shoes.
Key history findings include plantar foot pain which increases with walking, paresthesias and burning pain in the interspace between toes, and numbness (see ).

Typical physical examination findings include the presence of a Mulder's click (a palpable click noted with compression of the digital interspace just distal to the metatarsal heads), pain with digital pressure to the intermetatarsal space, and sensory loss in the affected toes. Gauthier's test involves squeezing the forefoot with medial to lateral pressure; in Morton's neuroma this should reproduce the symptoms.
In one study of 40 patients, the thumb index finger squeeze test was the most sensitive screening test for the clinical diagnosis of Morton’s neuroma.
Pain over the metatarsal heads should prompt consideration of metatarsalgia as an alternate diagnosis.
Imaging is generally not necessary in a patient with typical symptoms, although it is appropriate to order plain radiographs to rule out other pathology when the diagnosis is uncertain.

On ultrasound examination, the neuroma causes a hypoechoic signal in an ovoid mass. In one study, asymptomatic thickenings >5 mm in diameter (termed sonographic neuromas) were found in 54% of 48 volunteers. In 17 cases, enlarged nerves were found bilaterally.
MRI can detect lesions of the interdigital nerve in asymptomatic patients (ie, produce false-positive results), so clinical correlation of MRI with symptoms is necessary.

Authors of a systematic review of 12 small studies found that ultrasound provides better diagnostic accuracy than MRI. A more recent meta-analysis of 14 studies, however, found similar diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound and MRI; ultrasound would be more cost-effective.

Clinical assessment is the most accurate method for making the diagnosis and estimating lesion size. Preoperative clinical evaluation by the surgeon is 100% sensitive, MRI is 79% sensitive, and ultrasound is 86% sensitive.
Provide patient education concerning Morton's neuroma and outline treatment options.
Ensure that the patient wears comfortable shoes that accommodate the forefoot without compression.
Fit the patient with a metatarsal pad placed in the shoes proximal to the inflamed nerve.
Offer a corticosteroid injection if the above measures do not relieve symptoms by at least 50% in 3 months.
Reinforce the importance of proper footwear and continue a metatarsal pad for 3 additional months.
Consider surgical consultation with a podiatrist or foot and ankle surgeon for persistent symptoms despite conservative treatment for 6 months.
Initial conservative treatment (avoiding tight or high-heeled shoes and using metatarsal pads) is successful approximately 50% of the time. B
No randomized controlled trial evidence exists to support the use of orthotics to pronate or supinate the foot. B
A single corticosteroid injection can relieve symptoms for patients with an interdigital neuroma.B
A high proportion (80%) of patients who underwent nerve excision through a dorsal approach reported a greater than 50% reduction in pain with an average follow-up of 3.1 years. B
There is no clear randomized controlled trial evidence to recommend for or against the use of nonsteroidal medication in the treatment of Morton's neuroma.

A single corticosteroid injection can relieve symptoms for patients with an interdigital neuroma. In one small study, injection was better tolerated using a dorsal vs. plantar approach. Use of preliminary local anesthesia did not appear to confer additional benefit. Ultrasound guidance for injection did not improve outcome in one RCT, but did in another.

A small Brazilian study randomized 44 patients to receive 3 weekly injections either of hyaluronic acid (Osteonil Plus 40 mg/2 mL; n = 22 patients, 24 feet) or triamcinolone hexacetonide (Triancil 40 mg/2 mL; n = 22 patients, 24 feet). Patients who received corticosteroid injections experienced significantly greater pain reduction than those who received hyaluronic acid injections (at the expense of skin discoloration). Since pain was the primary outcome, the lack of a placebo group is a serious omission.
A Cochrane review found 6 RCTs with 373 patients. They found the strongest evidence for ultrasound guided injections of corticosteroids and local anesthetic.

A systematic review of studies with a wide range of validity concluded that corticosteroid injections were the most likely to be effective, with possible benefit from alcohol injection. A second systematic review comparing injections with surgery concluded that surgery was more likely to be effective. However, the quality of included studies was poor and consists largely of case series.

Evidence is limited in support of injecting sclerosing alcohol to treat Morton’s neuroma. In a single small study, investigators reported a 69% success rate using ultrasound-guided alcohol injection. In a second small study of 87 patients, investigators reported similar results for alcohol ablation with partial or complete treatment response in 66% (32% had complete pain resolution) at a mean follow-up of 14.3 months.

Complete resection of the nerve is the primary surgical intervention for Morton's neuroma. A systematic review found some evidence that transposition of the transected plantar digital nerve is more effective than standard resection.

A dorsal approach may lessen the risk of postoperative pain; however, a RCT of 76 patients did not find significant differences with regard to pain, daily activity restriction, or scar tenderness between a plantar vs. dorsal approach and good outcomes were observed in 87% (plantar) and 83% (dorsal) of patients.

Neuroablation using cryotherapy has been recommended, but clinical trials are lacking. In a series of 25 patients treated with ultrasound-guided radiofrequency ablation, following an average number of treatment sessions of 1.6 (range 1-3), there was a significant reduction in pain scores by VAS following treatment and again at 6 months. Overall, 26 out of 30 feet had a satisfactory outcome. In another case series with 29 patients, 83% had complete symptom relief at an average follow-up of 13 months following radiofrequency thermoneurolysis therapy.
A case series reported good results for minimally-invasive distal metatarsal metaphyseal osteotomy and percutaneous release of the deep transverse metatarsal ligament as an alternative to neurectomy.
Initial conservative treatment is to discontinue wearing tight or high-heeled shoes and to use a metatarsal pad, although these interventions have not been studied in clinical trials.
Conservative treatment has been shown to be successful for approximately half of patients with interdigital neuroma.
Using orthotics to pronate or supinate the foot is not effective for Morton's neuroma.

Authors of a systematic review found no or limited evidence for extracorporeal shockwave therapy, Botox, cryoneurolysis, or radiofrequency ablation. The strongest evidence supported corticosteroid injection.

Of 41 patients undergoing neurectomy through a dorsal approach for Morton’s neuroma, 76% had very good results in subjective and objective patient assessments, six (15%) had good results, one (2%) had satisfactory results and three (7%) had poor results over an average follow-up of 7.4 years (range: 5-12 years).
Avoid high heels or tight shoes; wear wider shoes with lower heels and a soft sole.
